title: Why do you see spots after looking at a bright light?

cards.title: The flash is over in an instant. The spot it leaves is not.
cards.text: Someone takes your photo with a flash, and for the next few seconds a dark spot floats in the middle of everything you look at. Look at the wall: it's there. Look at the floor: it's there too. But there's nothing on the wall or the floor.

notes: A flash, then a dark spot on the wall and the floor

cards.title: A flash tires out a patch of cells in your eye
cards.text: It's in your eye. At the back of each eye is a layer of cells that turn light into signals for your brain. The flash hits a patch of those cells so hard that they get tired out. For a little while, they respond less to light than the cells around them.
cards.hook: So why does a tired patch show up as a dark spot?

notes: A flash tires out a patch of the layer of cells at the back of your eye

cards.title: Tired cells send weaker signals, so you see a dark spot
cards.text: Look at a plain wall. The cells around the patch send signals for the wall as usual, but the tired cells send weaker ones. Your brain gets a normal picture with a dark spot in it.
cards.hook: So why does the spot follow your eyes?

notes: Normal cells: strong signal, tired cells: weak signal, what you see: a dark spot

cards.title: The spot follows your eyes because it's part of your eye
cards.text: It's tied to that part of your eye, not to anything out there. A few seconds later, when the cells recover, it fades.
cards.takeaway: The spot isn't in the room. It's a patch of your eye that got tired out by the flash.

notes: The spot turns with your eye, then fades as the cells recover

cards.note: Look at the spot against a far wall and it seems big; against your hand it seems small. The patch on your eye never changes size. Only your brain's guess at its size does.
